summary: AutoMat packages 85 SME-curated computational materials science claims (from 10 papers, several co-authored by the authors) as unsupervised reproduction tasks: the agent gets the claim, paper, metadata and optional artifacts and must rebuild and run the workflow on an HPC node. Five settings (Claude Code with Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 or Kimi K2.5; Codex CLI with GPT-5.4; and the authors' phased orchestrated agent on Sonnet 4.6) are scored by a tool-using LLM evaluator calibrated against blinded SMEs (QWK 0.69, n=40). The best setting succeeds on 53% of claims, from-paper tasks are far harder than from-artifact tasks, and the orchestrated workflow gives no overall gain over Claude Code on the same backbone.

claims.claim: Best setting (Claude Code + Opus 4.6) reaches 53% success; Codex + GPT-5.4 is weakest at 23%
claims.evidence: Fig. 4 mean scores 3.52 vs 2.44 and success rates. One run per claim per setting; scores come from the LLM evaluator, which is conservative vs SMEs (bias -0.325, Table 9), so absolute rates may be understated.

claims.claim: Reconstructing a workflow from paper text alone is the main bottleneck; executable artifacts make tasks much easier
claims.evidence: Fig. 5: from-paper mean 1.5-3.0 with near-zero success except CC/Opus; from-artifact 3.0-4.0 and 37-71% success. Claim sets differ across reproduction types (no within-claim manipulation of artifact access), and judge agreement is lowest on from-paper tasks (QWK 0.59, n=15).

claims.claim: Task-specific orchestration does not improve overall reproduction over a general-purpose agent
claims.evidence: Fig. 6 paired per-claim comparison on Sonnet 4.6: 44.7% ties, wins and losses balanced; Table 12: only scientific rigor is directional (one-sided p=0.038, two-sided p=0.076). Same backbone, 85 paired claims, but one run each, so the null is underpowered rather than proven.

claims.claim: Failures are dominated by procedural incompleteness and methodological deviation rather than code generation
claims.evidence: Fig. 7 heatmap of evaluator-assigned failure labels. Evaluator-SME agreement on these labels is only example-F1 0.61 on 73 runs (Table 11), lower for Codex and Kimi; authors call them aggregate diagnostics.

claims.claim: A no-execution reader understands claims but misses execution-critical parameters
claims.evidence: App. I: Opus 4.6 read-only baseline scores 4.88/5 claim comprehension but 3.83 parameter fidelity; 28/85 claims high comprehension with low method/parameter scores. Single model, evaluator not calibrated for this setting.

patterns.note: Fixed four-phase workflow (read-only plan -> environment setup -> deterministic execution with LLM failure diagnosis -> result extraction) compared against Claude Code on the same Sonnet 4.6 backbone over 85 paired claims: no overall gain (44.7% ties, balanced wins/losses), directional rigor gain only, fewer overconfidence labels but more resource/execution failures. A reasonable comparison in which the fixed workflow does not win.

In the orchestrated agent the LLM planner declares steps with dependencies that a Python orchestrator topologically sorts and runs with timeouts and up to 3 diagnosed retries (App. C.4). Bundled with the P36 phases, so the same no-overall-gain comparison applies and the DAG itself is not isolated.

The orchestrated agent's read-only planning phase is discovery before action, but it is not isolated. App. I shows static reading of paper plus artifacts made tasks look understood (4.88/5 comprehension) while missing execution-critical details on 28/85 claims. No discovery strategies are compared.

Tool-using evaluator agent given hidden SME reference steps. Agreement with blinded SMEs: QWK 0.69 overall (n=40), 0.59 on from-paper tasks, systematic conservative bias -0.33; failure-mode labels F1 0.61 (n=73). Calibration SMEs were the authors of the source studies.
New claim-level scientific reproduction benchmark with released tasks, harness and prompts.
Agent works on a sandboxed copy of the visible payload; evaluation-only materials are kept outside via symlink separation. Not evaluated as a harness choice.

methodology.sample: 85 claims from 10 papers (96 annotated, 11 dropped in QC); 5 agent settings; 40-run SME calibration subset; 73-run failure-label audit
methodology.baselines: Off-the-shelf Claude Code and Codex CLI; orchestrated agent vs Claude Code on the same backbone; read-only no-execution diagnostic
methodology.models: Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Kimi K2.5 (in Claude Code 2.1.78); GPT-5.4 high (Codex CLI 0.115.0); orchestrated agent on Claude Agent SDK + Sonnet 4.6
methodology.variance: One run per claim per setting; standard errors across claims in Fig. 5; paired Wilcoxon tests for RQ2; agent run-to-run variance not measured
methodology.ablations: Orchestrated vs free-form on the same model; no-execution diagnostic; individual orchestration phases not ablated
methodology.contamination_controls: URLs stripped from papers; SME procedure kept outside the sandbox. The paper text (with target numbers) is given to the agent by design, and 'circular reasoning' (hardcoding paper values) is a scored failure mode.
methodology.languages: Python plus scientific toolchains (Quantum ESPRESSO, LAMMPS) on Slurm/HPC; no general software engineering tasks

standards.artifacts: Code (GitHub JHU-CLSP/AutoMat), dataset (Hugging Face), prompts in App. E
standards.preregistration: n/a (one-sided test described as pre-specified, not registered)

biases.detail: Claims come from only 10 source papers; judge calibration uses 40 runs (12-15 per reproduction type).
Single run per claim and setting; agent stochasticity is not measured, so the 53% vs 23% spread and the RQ2 null carry unknown run-level noise.
Several source studies are by co-authors, and each calibration run was scored by the SME who authored the source study (App. A, H.1).
No tokens, dollars or wall-clock per run, despite runs of up to 72 h on 96-core nodes.
Workflows are Python plus domain simulation codes; nothing about typed, multi-service codebases.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Kimi K2.5; no author has a vendor affiliation
coi.funding: DARPA HR001125C0304, ONR N0001424-1-2089, NSF OAC1920103 (compute)
coi.detail: No vendor ties. Mild self-curation: co-authors supplied source studies and scored calibration runs. The authors' own orchestrated agent does not win, so there is no self-promotion.

verdict_reason: Credible benchmark with an SME-calibrated judge, released artifacts and a clean same-backbone null result on a fixed phased workflow. Caveats: single runs, one scientific domain, judge conservative and weakest on the hardest task type, and only indirect relevance to software teams.
applicability: Indirect. For a discovery or onboarding harness, the from-paper vs from-artifact gap and the App. I reader show that prose documentation alone can make a task look understood while execution-critical parameters stay missing. Discovery steps should point agents and new developers at runnable artifacts (sample ingestion runs, fixtures, real configs) and have them execute those artifacts, not only read docs. The null result on a fixed read-only-plan-first workflow is a caution against assuming a rigid discovery phase improves outcomes by itself. Does not transfer directly: scientific HPC workflows in Python, no Java services, no multi-repo coordination.

conflicts_with.detail: 2606.18051 reports a fixed decompose-retrieve-compose pipeline beating a ReAct loop on the same model; AutoMat finds a fixed phased workflow gives no overall gain over a free-form agent loop on the same backbone. Domains differ (MCP tool routing vs scientific reproduction), so the disagreement is about how far fixed workflows generalize.
